questions.problem:
Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ be eigenvectors of a matrix $A$ that correspond to eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ respectively.
What is the general solution of the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution of our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the system of differential equations 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-4{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

*Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}].$

- We are given that the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-1\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=1.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ -4 & 4\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ be eigenvectors of a matrix $A.$ Find the decoupling matrix of the differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we construct the matrix $E$, whose columns are the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
E=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, the decoupling matrix can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={E}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot (-3)}[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the substitution that will decouple the following system of differential equations: 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].$

- Since $A$ is lower-triangular, the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-3\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, we have $E=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, the change of variables that decouples the system is given by $x(t)=Eu(t)$, or equivalently,

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t)=-{u}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)={u}_{1}(t)+{u}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Decoupling Substitution of a Linear System of Differential Equations
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the substitution that will decouple the following system of differential equations: 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's construct the matrix differential equation $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)$ for the given system:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067055/assets/cd09988206ce7738d335cf25814f9820d5003c286904c8e136e55724f2fc1185.png)

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A.$

- Since $A$ is lower-triangular, the eigenvalues are 

$$
\lambda_1=-3
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\lambda_2=1.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For $\lambda_1 =-3,$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067055/assets/9bd0bffeaccd9f7523829b9f385c5e75a25ecd663877f0b5711d271938e484e6.png)
So, we get an eigenvector 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067055/assets/0683c697abc42c91bc62d5f52aafa1fd7b79cd5156e999b3aac4802d9359773e.png)

- For $\lambda_2 =1,$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067055/assets/816a9a9b4948cae2d5a21b6e5ccf80928cadefb4d8a7ca1d333166b2fe66e5ac.png)
So, we get an eigenvector 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067055/assets/491ab9ee9c59586dbccb6c043a3225adc3ef95496c056d37891594513f1f6069.png)

Therefore, we have ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067055/assets/6c51e641ebd7c4e64366c23aa9c7e091c3b711724069b47b104dc6f1c588f7bc.png)

Finally, the change of variables that decouples the system is given by $\mathbf{x}(t) = E\mathbf{u}(t),$ or equivalently,

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t)=4{u}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)=3{u}_{1}(t)+{u}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$
